title: Forgiving someone
hookLine: where there is forgiveness, there the Lord is, says Kabir (Kabir salok, ang 1372)
tomorrow: simran versions a clapback. what does maya's grandma say?

cards: Tara's story goes up at 7:02 in the morning. A blurry photo of Simran at lunch, and three words over it: fake nice girl. Then a crying-laughing face.
Half the grade sees it before first period. Simran feels it in her stomach first, then in her jaw. Her dad, Harjit, driving her to school, sees her face and turns the radio down.
You don't have to forgive her by second period, he says. But someday you'll want to put it down.

teach.b: Kabir has a short salok near the end of the Guru Granth Sahib that reads like a map. Where there is compassion, there is dharma, the right way. Where there is greed, there is sin.

teach.h: WHERE THERE IS ANGER, THERE IS DEATH.
teach.b: Where there is anger, there is death. And where there is forgiveness, there the Lord is, himself. Look at what it sets side by side.
Anger isn't called rude. It's called death, something that keeps taking from the one who holds it. And forgiveness isn't called nice.
It's where God is found. That's the line to tell a friend tonight: in Kabir's map, forgiveness is a place, and the Lord lives there. Now what forgiveness isn't.
It isn't pretending nothing happened. It isn't letting someone keep hurting you. Simran can still tell a teacher, still mute Tara, still say this was wrong.
Forgiveness works on the anger itself: putting down the wish for Tara to hurt back.
Sheikh Farid, also in the Granth, pushes further: answer evil with good, and don't let anger settle in your mind.
So it isn't a switch flipped at 7:15. Simran doesn't feel forgiving yet. But that night she deletes the reply she'd drafted.

how: Kabir's salok on Ang 1372 places the Lord where forgiveness is, and Sikh teaching adds that forgiving doesn't mean excusing harm or staying in harm's way.

o: letting go of the wish for them to hurt back
agreeing that what they did was okay
forgetting what they did as fast as you can

p: don't let anger settle in the mind

s: forgiving someone means acting like it never happened
you can still say it was wrong and protect yourself; forgiveness lets go of hurting back.
Kabir's salok says where there is anger, there is death
anger keeps taking from the one who holds it.

games.q: your friend's brother dented her car and apologized. a week later she's still furious, and feels like a bad person for it. what does Kabir's salok offer her?
o: forgiveness is a place to head toward; it can take time and still be real.
if she really forgave him, the anger would be gone by now.
forgiving him means handing him the keys again right away.
games.why: Kabir puts the Lord where forgiveness is. it isn't pretending or handing back the keys; it's putting down the wish to hurt back, at a human pace.

practice: Close your eyes and bring to mind someone you're still angry with; not the worst thing, something you can hold.
Notice where the anger sits in your body, and with each out-breath let a little of its grip loosen, without deciding they were right. If it won't loosen today, that's honest too.

wordCard.voice: Forgiving someone. Putting down the wish for them to hurt back. Khima is the word in Kabir's salok.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: khima, forgiveness; where there is khima, Kabir says, there the Lord is.

carryVoice: Your line: where there is forgiveness. Kabir finishes it: there the Lord is. Go gently.

sources.ref: Ang 1372 (Salok Kabir: jahaa daiaa tah dharam hai, jahaa lobh tah paap; jahaa krodh tah kaal hai, jahaa khima tah aap), paraphrased
Ang 1381–1382 (Salok Farid: Farida buray da bhala kar, gussa man na hadhaae), paraphrased
